title: Two verses on the wall
hookLine: the head monk writes that the mind is a mirror to be wiped; Huineng answers that there is no mirror stand

cards: Late at night, by lamplight, a monk walks down a corridor with a brush and ink. He writes a short verse on the wall and goes back to his room without signing it. In the morning the whole monastery is reading it.

The teacher Hongren had set a test: write a verse that shows your understanding, and whoever truly understands will receive the robe and become the next teacher in the line. Everyone expected the head monk to win.

teach.b: First, the mirror to be wiped. The head monk was Shenxiu, a respected teacher in his own right.
His verse, in the Platform Sutra, says roughly this: the body is the tree of awakening, the mind is like a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it clean, again and again, and don't let dust gather.
It's a beautiful picture of practice: steady, patient care.

Second, a verse he can't write. In the threshing room, Huineng hears a boy chanting Shenxiu's lines. He can't read, so he asks someone to read the wall to him, and then asks someone to write his own answer beside it.
Third, no tree, no stand. Huineng's verse turns Shenxiu's around: awakening has no tree, the bright mirror has no stand. Here the versions of the Platform Sutra differ.

The older one found at Dunhuang says Buddha-nature is always clean and pure; later versions say that from the beginning there is not a single thing. Both end with the same question: where could the dust land?
Fourth, what the two pictures mean.
Shenxiu describes the mind as something to keep polishing.
Huineng says the clear nature was never dirty in the first place. That night Hongren calls Huineng in secret, gives him the robe, and sends him south.
Later Chan writers told the story as gradual against sudden, and it comes to us from Huineng's side.
But both verses are still read, and some readers find room for both in practice: some wiping, and some moments of seeing there was nothing to wipe.

how: Chan and Zen students learn both verses, Shenxiu's and Huineng's, and teachers use them to talk about steady practice and the mind's original clarity.

games.q: you're Huineng. you have an answer to the head monk's verse, but you can't read or write. what do you do?
o: keep quiet; it's not your place.

games.why: Huineng asked someone to read him the wall, then to write his answer beside it. that night Hongren gave him the robe.

practice: If there's a mirror or a phone screen nearby, wipe it slowly and watch the smudges go: that's Shenxiu's patient, honest work. Then close your eyes and notice what's aware of the breath right now.
Rest a few breaths with Huineng's question, where does dust land, without needing an answer.

wordCard.voice: Huineng. The monk whose verse answered Shenxiu's on the monastery wall: no tree, no stand, and nowhere for dust to land.
